name: Fish odor syndrome choline restriction

lead: Trimethylaminuria, or fish odor syndrome, is a rare condition in which a fishy-smelling compound builds up and appears in sweat, urine and breath. Choline restriction is one dietary approach described to ease the smell.

A deficient FMO3 enzyme fails to convert trimethylamine into an odourless form, and diets high in choline or carnitine supply more raw material. Most cases are inherited. Wikipedia says there is no known permanent cure and that symptoms are usually managed through diet.

paras: People with the condition work with medical or nutritional supervision to lower foods rich in choline and related compounds. It is used as a management approach for the condition rather than a general grooming tactic.

Choline is an essential nutrient, so Wikipedia says complete elimination is not advised and restriction is cautioned against in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Management is described as best done under medical or nutritional supervision.

angle.text: People with trimethylaminuria, a rare condition that gives sweat and breath a fishy smell, use choline restriction to give the body less raw material for the smelly compound. It is part of medically supervised management rather than a general grooming tactic.

lead: Trimethylaminuria (TMAU), also called fish odor syndrome, is a rare metabolic condition in which the body cannot adequately convert trimethylamine, a compound that smells like rotting fish, into odourless trimethylamine N-oxide.[1] Choline restriction is one dietary approach discussed for managing it. People with the condition and clinicians pursue it to control body odour, which affects how a person smells in daily and social life.[1]

Most cases are inherited through mutations in the FMO3 gene. Wikipedia says there is no known permanent cure, and symptoms are usually managed through diet under medical or nutritional supervision.[1] The odour is intermittent and tracks diet, and the condition is often unrecognised or mistaken for olfactory reference syndrome.[1]
On T Nation, a thread about fixing bad body odour mentions TMAU as a real condition, and a thread asking whether fish oils make you smell receives the reply that a person might have it.[2][3]
infobox: FMO3 deficiency (primary); high precursor intake or organ failure (secondary)[1]
Fishy odour in urine, sweat, breath

paras: The FMO3 enzyme normally oxidises trimethylamine; when deficient, it accumulates and is released in urine, sweat and breath. More than 40 mutations have been linked to the primary form, which is autosomal recessive. Secondary forms can follow very high supplement intake of precursors such as choline, carnitine or betaine, or liver or kidney failure.[1] Odour is intermittent and tracks diet over the previous day or so, and the condition appears to be more common in women and may worsen around puberty, menstruation, oral contraceptive use and menopause.[1]
The condition can bring shame, social isolation and low mood, and is frequently unrecognised or misdiagnosed.[1]

Wikipedia lists avoiding seafood and seaweed and reducing red meat and offal, which are high in carnitine, as common measures.[1] Reducing choline-rich foods such as fish, red meat, egg yolks, legumes and dairy may help, but complete elimination is not advised, and people who are pregnant or breastfeeding are cautioned not to restrict choline because it supports neural development.[1] Case reports and small studies have examined riboflavin, short-course antibiotics, slightly acidic soaps and activated charcoal with copper chlorophyllin.[1]

Screening measures the ratio of trimethylamine to its oxide in urine, and genetic testing is available, though some common FMO3 variants are considered benign. Urinary tract infections, bacterial vaginosis, advanced liver or kidney disease and some other conditions can cause false positives. Olfactory reference syndrome, a persistent false belief about one's odour, is often mistaken for TMAU.[1]
Wikipedia notes media attention to a singer in 2014 and appearances of the condition in television and film.[1] Forum users mention TMAU when discussing body odour problems and diet.[2][3]

Evidence cited by Wikipedia is limited to case reports and small studies, including riboflavin in two children and a Japanese study of charcoal with copper chlorophyllin; no large trial of choline restriction was found.[1]

timeline.event: First clinical case described, in a 6-year-old girl with elevated urinary trimethylamine.[1]
